title: Capacity factor

definition.text: The ratio of the electricity a power plant actually produces over a period to what it would produce running at full rated power the whole time.

facts.text: It can be computed for any power plant or class of plants, and is used to compare different kinds of electricity generation.
It is usually calculated over a year to average out fluctuations, though monthly values show seasonal swings.
A plant needed only from 8 am to 8 pm, even at full power every day, would have a 50% capacity factor.
Nuclear plants sit at the high end, about 88.7% on average for US plants over 2006–2012; typical wind farms run between 25 and 45%.
For wind, solar and hydro, the main limit is whether the 'fuel' of wind, sunlight or water is available.
Photovoltaic plants are at the low end, from 29.1% at an Arizona plant to 12.0% at one in Bavaria, because output depends on daylight and latitude.
Peaking plants have low capacity factors, so their electricity is relatively expensive: few hours of output must cover their fixed costs.

related: Base load and peaking power plants

title: Base load and peaking power plants
article: Capacity factor#Determinants of a plant capacity factor

definition.text: The split between power plants run continuously at high output and plants switched on only when demand is high.

facts.text: Base load plants are designed for maximum efficiency and run continuously, so their cost per unit of electricity is usually low.
Geothermal, nuclear, coal and solid-fuel bioenergy plants are almost always run as base load because their output is hard to adjust.
Peaking plants may run only a few hours a year, or several hours a day, when electricity is needed and prices are high enough.

definition.text: Changes in how much electricity customers use, made to better match demand to the available supply.

facts.text: Instead of adjusting power plant output, it adjusts demand in real time, and can be seen as a technology-enabled rationing system for electricity.
Utilities signal customers through cheaper off-peak rates or smart meters that send price changes, and customers respond by delaying power-hungry tasks or paying more.
Most consumers pay a fixed average price, so their short-run use does not respond to the real cost of production.
It can be cheaper than building extra generating capacity to meet peaks and occasional demand spikes.
A study found a 1% shift in peak demand would save 3.9%, and a 5% cut in demand might have halved peak prices in California's 2000–2001 electricity crisis.
Controlling flexible loads helps smooth the swings in output from wind and solar, and heat pumps can serve as such a flexible resource.
There is an economic limit, because consumers lose the productive or convenience value of electricity they do not use.

title: Peak demand
article: Demand response#Electricity grids and peak demand response

definition.text: The highest level of electricity use on a grid, which sets how much generating capacity must be built.

facts.text: Because supply and demand must balance at every moment, total capacity is sized to the peak plus a safety margin.
Peaks occur only a few times a year, so the plants and lines built for them sit mostly idle, and customers pay for that idle capacity.
One coalition estimated that 10%–20% of US electricity costs come from peak demand in only 100 hours of the year.

related: Base load and peaking power plants

definition.text: Deliberately cutting power to some users when generating capacity falls below demand.

facts.text: Utilities may use targeted or rolling blackouts, or agreements with big industrial users to switch off at system-wide peaks.
Users may be rewarded for firm commitments to cut use at peak times; such saved power is called negawatts, a term coined by Amory Lovins in 1985.
Industrial plants are well suited because their loads are large and they already have control systems.

definition.text: Reducing the amount of energy needed to provide the same products and services.

facts.text: Insulating a building, for example, lets it stay comfortable while using less energy for heating and cooling.
Its two main motives are saving operating costs and cutting greenhouse gas emissions; it can also reduce dependence on imported energy.
Efficient technology usually carries an upfront capital cost, and the costs can be compared using life-cycle assessment.
Energy policy increasingly treats it as the 'first fuel': the IEA found efficiency measures over 1974–2010 avoided more energy use in member states than any single fuel supplied.
Better efficiency in buildings, industry and transport could cut the world's energy needs in 2050 by one third, and the IEA estimates it could deliver 40% of the emission cuts the Paris goals need.
Its extra benefits, such as cleaner air, better health and energy security, have sometimes been valued above the energy savings themselves.
California's efficiency standards from the mid-1970s kept its per-capita energy use about flat while US consumption doubled.
Policies to promote it include carbon taxes, efficiency standards for appliances, buildings and vehicles, and subsidies for efficient equipment.

definition.text: The tendency for efficiency gains to save less energy than expected because they make energy services cheaper, so people use more of them.

facts.text: Fuel-efficient cars make travel cheaper, so drivers may go farther and offset part of the savings.
Estimates range from roughly 5% to 40%, likely under 30% for households and nearer 10% for transport.
A 30% rebound means an efficiency gain delivers 70% of the energy savings engineering models predict.
Historical analysis shows efficiency gains were almost always outpaced by economic growth, so total resource use and pollution still rose.

definition.text: Actively using less energy, through changes in behaviour as well as through more efficient technology.

facts.text: Examples without any efficiency gain include heating a room less, driving less, air-drying clothes and using a computer's power-saving mode.
The line between conservation and efficiency can be fuzzy, but both matter environmentally and economically.
Energy conservation sits at the top of the sustainable energy hierarchy.
Burning fossil fuels for transport and electricity is less than 50% efficient, with much heat wasted.

definition.text: The amount of energy an economy uses per unit of GDP or other economic output.

facts.text: It differs from energy efficiency: climate, economic structure such as services versus manufacturing, and trade all affect it.
Cold or hot climates raise it through heating and cooling needs, and higher living standards bring more energy-using goods.
Using 2003–2004 figures, the US used 8,553 BTU per dollar of GDP, Bangladesh about a quarter of that, and Russia more than double.
Its inverse, economic energy efficiency, counts GDP produced per unit of energy; the change in energy use needed to raise a country's GDP over time is its energy elasticity.
It is one of the four factors in the Kaya identity, alongside population, GDP per capita and carbon intensity of energy.
Global energy intensity has generally fallen over recent decades with better efficiency, technology and shifts in economic structure.
Official statistics count only commercially marketed energy, so firewood, charcoal and similar small sources are left out.

definition.text: Lack of access to modern energy services, such as electricity and clean cooking fuel, in the home.

facts.text: In 2024 an estimated 655 million people had no electricity and about two billion cooked with polluting fuels and technologies.
Its causes include missing infrastructure such as power plants, lines and pipelines, and prices that poorer households cannot afford.
It harms health, education and women's opportunities; household air pollution caused about 2.9 million deaths in 2021, by the WHO's estimate.
Women and children in homes using wood, charcoal or dung do most of the cooking and fuel collection, so they bear most of the health burden.
Ninety percent of children in Sub-Saharan Africa attend primary schools without electricity.
In the Global North it is usually called fuel poverty: households that cannot afford to heat, cool and power their homes because of high prices, low incomes and inefficient appliances.
There is no agreed standard for basic energy services and no single indicator accepted internationally, so measures range from yes-or-no access to composite indices.
Clean, efficient cook stoves running on LPG or electricity are a recommended low-cost way to cut its health harms.

definition.text: A composite index that classes people as energy poor according to how many kinds of energy deprivation they face.

facts.text: Its seven indicators are access to light, modern cooking fuel, fresh air, refrigeration, recreation, communication and space cooling.
It multiplies the share of people who are energy poor by the average intensity of their deprivation, capturing both breadth and depth.
Other indices include the IEA's Energy Development Index, which tracks a country's shift to modern fuels, and the household-level Energy Poverty Index.

definition.text: The link between a nation's security and the reliable availability of energy resources.

facts.text: Modern economies depend on affordable energy, and the uneven spread of supplies among countries creates serious vulnerabilities.
Threats include instability in producing countries, supply manipulation, and attacks on pipelines and grids.
The 1973 oil crisis and the rise of the OPEC cartel pushed countries such as Japan to diversify into gas, nuclear power, mass transit and conservation.
Imported natural gas creates sharper short-term risks than oil, as the Russia–Ukraine gas disputes of 2006 and 2009 showed.
Wind, solar and efficiency are spread across many countries, unlike fossil fuels, so deploying them and diversifying sources raises energy security.
Carefully phasing out fossil fuel subsidies would increase energy security, according to the International Institute for Sustainable Development.
Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine made energy security a stronger driver of the energy transition in Europe.

definition.text: The ability of an energy system to adjust to and withstand interruptions in supply.

facts.text: Some argue energy independence is unrealistic, and resilience is a more practical goal.
The 1982 book Brittle Power argued the real weakness is centralised, interdependent infrastructure, and recommended decentralised efficiency and renewables.
A diverse supply is less affected when any one source is disrupted.

definition.text: A government stockpile of oil held as a buffer against the economic and political shocks of an energy crisis.

facts.text: All 31 members of the International Energy Agency hold at least 90 days of their oil imports.
These countries also committed to emergency response plans for oil supply shocks.

definition.text: The pattern in which the cost of making something falls by a steady share each time the total amount ever produced doubles.

facts.text: In 1936 engineer Theodore Paul Wright found that each doubling of total aircraft production cut the labour needed for a new aircraft by 20%, now called Wright's law.
Other industries show reductions from a couple of percent up to 30% per doubling, usually constant within each industry.
Bruce Henderson of the Boston Consulting Group coined the term 'experience curve' from cost studies in the 1960s.
Causes include workers' growing skill, standardisation and specialisation, new technology, fuller use of equipment and product redesign.
It implies firms gain by expanding early: more output brings learning, lower costs and prices, and larger market share.
Storage costs follow such curves: lithium-ion battery prices fall 19% with each doubling of capacity, while pumped hydro has barely fallen.
Critics note that experience effects are tangled with economies of scale and may be hard to separate.

title: Wright's law
article: Experience curve effect#Wright's law unit cost curve

definition.text: A power-law formula in which unit cost falls by a fixed proportion, the learning rate, with each doubling of cumulative production.

facts.text: The progress ratio b gives the remaining share of cost after each doubling, and one minus b is the learning rate.
Across many industries b ranges from 0.75 to 0.9, so costs fall 10% to 25% per doubling.
A curve with a 15% cut per doubling is called an '85% experience curve'.
The exponent is a statistical estimate, so it cannot exactly predict any future unit's cost.

definition.text: Technologies connected to the power grid that store electricity for later use.

facts.text: It balances supply and demand by storing surplus power from variable renewables such as solar and inflexible sources such as nuclear, then releasing it when needed.
Storage is one of the three main ways to replace the flexibility fossil fuels have given the grid.
As of 2023 pumped hydro was the largest form, at 181 GW, ahead of about 88 GW of batteries combined.
Lithium-ion batteries suit storage of under 8 hours; flow batteries and compressed air suit medium durations; hydrogen and heat suit seasonal storage.
Battery costs fell by 90% from 2010 to 2023.
Below 40% variable renewables only short storage under 4 hours is needed; at 80% medium-duration storage is needed, and above 90% long-duration storage.
It can also help restart the grid after a blackout.

definition.text: Storing electricity by pumping water uphill to a reservoir when demand is low and releasing it through turbines when demand peaks.

facts.text: It was the largest form of grid storage in 2023, with 181 GW installed worldwide.
It is 75% to 85% efficient and responds within seconds to minutes, which suits daily swings in demand.
It expanded fast during the 1960s–1980s nuclear boom because nuclear plants cannot quickly follow demand.

title: Economics of energy storage
article: Grid energy storage#Market and system value

definition.text: How storage earns money and what it costs, measured over its lifetime and against the services it provides to the grid.

facts.text: The levelized cost of storage is lifetime cost per MWh discharged, including investment, operating and charging costs.
Storage earns value from power quality, reliability, better use of grid assets, and arbitrage between low and high prices, which has the largest potential.
More storage on the market shrinks price gaps, so storage 'cannibalises' its own income even more than renewables do.
Because storage loses some energy, small price differences may not justify charging and discharging; demand response or grid expansion may be cheaper options.

definition.text: The average cost of electricity from a generator over its lifetime, expressed in today's money per unit of energy produced.

facts.text: It is the constant price per unit of energy that would give the project a net present value of zero.
It divides the discounted sum of investment, maintenance and fuel costs by the discounted sum of electricity produced over the plant's life.
It is used to compare generating technologies on a consistent basis for investment planning and energy policy.
It estimates the cost of production, not the price of electricity, which also reflects markups and price controls.
The discount rate is one of its most contested inputs: public comparisons tend to use about 3%, private banks 7–15%, and low rates favour nuclear and renewables with high upfront costs.
Since 2013 the LCOE of wind has been below that of all fossil fuels, and solar followed in 2015.
It ignores when power is produced, so wind and solar without storage may generate when electricity is worth little or even negative.
It often leaves out indirect costs such as the social cost of greenhouse gases and air pollution, as well as co-benefits.

definition.text: The discounted costs a new generator would avoid, divided by its discounted lifetime output, used as a measure of its value to the grid.

facts.text: In 2014 the US Energy Information Administration recommended comparing wind and solar costs with this measure rather than with fossil plants' LCOE.
Its ratio to the LCOE is the value-cost ratio; above 1, a project counts as economically feasible.
System LCOE and similar metrics instead add the cost of storage or backup plants needed when wind and solar are unavailable.

title: Merit order

definition.text: The ranking of power sources from cheapest to most expensive to run, which sets the order in which they are switched on to meet demand.

facts.text: Plants with the lowest short-run marginal costs are brought online first and the costliest last, which minimises the cost of producing electricity.
The marginal cost of the last generator needed to meet demand sets the system price for one more MWh.
In most power systems the wholesale price equals the marginal cost of the most expensive generator running, so prices often vary two- to fivefold over a day.
Plants sometimes run out of merit order because of transmission congestion or reliability needs.
Environmental dispatch adds the goal of minimising pollutant emissions to that of minimising fuel costs.
Policy-makers use marginal abatement cost curves in the same way, as merit order curves of emission-cutting options.

related: Base load and peaking power plants

title: Merit order effect
article: Merit order#The effect of renewable energy on merit order

definition.text: The lowering of wholesale electricity prices when wind and solar, which have near-zero fuel costs, push expensive plants out of the merit order.

facts.text: Wind and solar have very low marginal costs because they pay nothing for fuel, so they are bought first and displace costly peak power.
A Fraunhofer ISI study found solar cut prices on the German exchange by 10% on average and up to 40% in the early afternoon.
In Germany 2008–2012, each extra GWh of renewables cut day-ahead prices by 0.11–0.13 ¢/kWh.
Solar peaks at noon while demand in warm climates peaks in late afternoon, producing the so-called duck curve.

definition.text: The short-term choice of how much each power plant should produce to meet load at the lowest possible cost within grid and operating limits.

facts.text: It can be framed as maximising the economic welfare of a power network subject to power balance and line capacity constraints, solved with Lagrange multipliers.
Transmission limits make the cost of one more MWh differ by location; these are called locational marginal prices.
The equations are nonlinear and hard to solve, so a simplified linear 'DC power flow' model is often used.

definition.text: The spot price of a barrel of benchmark crude oil, such as Brent or West Texas Intermediate, used as a reference by buyers and sellers.

facts.text: It is set by global supply and demand rather than any one country's output, though the OPEC cartel pushes prices up.
Prices were fairly steady from 1861 until the 1970s, when the 1973 and 1979 oil crises drove a significant rise.
Its main drivers have been supply, demand and storage shocks and shocks to global economic growth.
Oil peaked at US$147 in July 2008 and fell to US$34 by December 2008 as the financial crisis took hold.
The 2014–2016 drop of 70% after a supply glut was one of the three biggest declines since World War II.
High oil prices generally hurt global growth and raise the cost of many products, including food.
Production costs differ widely: in 2019 Middle Eastern oil broke even at about US$42 a barrel and oil sands at US$83.

title: 1970s oil crises
article: Price of oil#Global oil prices: a chronology

definition.text: The 1973 and 1979 oil supply shocks that sharply raised world oil prices and reshaped energy policy.

facts.text: In the 1973 crisis Arab oil producers embargoed shipments to Western Europe and the United States over their support for Israel.
In 1979 the Iranian Revolution constrained supply and the oil price more than doubled.
Countries such as the US, Germany, Japan and Canada responded with national energy programmes focused on secure oil supply.
The crises gave rise to speculative trading and crude oil futures markets.

title: Oil futures and speculation
article: Price of oil#Speculative trading and crude oil futures

definition.text: Contracts to buy or sell oil at a set future date, through which investors bet on oil prices and firms hedge against price swings.

facts.text: NYMEX launched crude oil futures in 1983 and the IPE in 1988, and world crude prices came to be published through these markets.
Futures helped reduce the economic hazards of swings in the spot price.
A 2008 US task force found the 2003–2008 price rise was due mainly to supply and demand, not speculation, given low price elasticity.
In the contango trade, companies buy cheap oil for storage and hold it until prices rise.

title: Variable renewable energy

definition.text: Renewable power sources such as wind and solar whose output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be adjusted on demand.

facts.text: Their traits are unpredictability, variability and low operating costs, which make matching supply and demand harder for grid operators.
Small amounts barely affect the grid, but large amounts may require upgrading or redesigning grid infrastructure.
Wind and solar supplied 15% of world electricity in 2024 and together overtook hydropower for the first time.
Integration options include storage, demand response, overcapacity, interconnecting grids and linking power with heat, transport and industry.
Spreading wind farms over wide areas lowers overall variability, because distant turbines' outputs are imperfectly correlated.
Combined wind and solar could reach 70% to 90% of supply without aggregation, demand management or storage, and up to 94% with 12 hours of storage.
The size of the extra costs of variability is debated, but they are small at low shares and expected to rise with higher shares.

contested_note: Sources call the magnitude of the economic costs of wind and solar variability debated, varying by location.

title: Operating reserve

definition.text: Spare generating capacity a grid keeps ready to follow changes in demand or replace generation that is suddenly lost.

facts.text: Capacity that can replace lost generation within about 30 seconds to 30 minutes is called spinning reserve.
Wind does not need 100% back-up, because reserves are calculated for the whole system rather than for each plant.
Thermal plants running as reserve or peakers are less efficient than when run as base load.

related: Base load and peaking power plants

definition.text: Linking the power system with transport, heating and gas so that demand and generation can be better matched.

facts.text: Electric vehicles are expected to become the largest source of storage capacity, charging when production is high and sometimes feeding power back to the grid.
The International Energy Agency says it is needed to handle the mismatch between seasonal demand and supply.
It may cost more than other flexibility options and suits grids with high shares of variable renewables.

definition.text: The study of how societies supply and use energy, and of the costs and value of energy services.

facts.text: Energy services are the end uses energy provides, such as lighting, heating and fuel, and the aim is to deliver them with the least energy input.
It is an applied branch of economics drawing on engineering, geology, political science and ecology, not a self-contained discipline.
Its topics include the elasticity of supply and demand in energy markets and the liberalisation and regulation of electricity markets.
Energy issues have been prominent in economics since the 1973 oil crisis, but W.S. Jevons worried about coal depletion as early as 1865.
Harold Hotelling's rule gave an early price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels.
Its theory has grown around three themes: the rebound effect, the energy efficiency gap and, more recently, green nudges.
Vaclav Smil argues every economic activity is at root a conversion of energy, with money only a rough proxy for valuing energy flows.

definition.text: Government interventions, such as feedback on energy bills, that steer energy users toward greener choices without forcing them.

facts.text: The term was coined by Thaler and Sunstein in 2008.
They respond to the finding that energy consumers do not behave fully rationally, something the energy efficiency gap idea leaves out.
They arose because the energy efficiency gap idea ignored consumers' behavioural quirks.
Energy economics research now focuses on influencing decisions to close the energy efficiency gap.

definition.text: Small, grid-connected devices that generate and store electricity close to the load they serve, called distributed energy resources.

facts.text: Conventional power stations are centralised and often send power over long distances, whereas distributed energy resources are modular, sited near the load and have capacities of 10 MW or less.
Central plants' economies of scale began to fail in the late 1960s, and by the early 21st century they arguably could no longer deliver cheap, reliable power to remote customers through the grid.

Distributed energy resources include cogeneration, solar photovoltaics, small wind, microhydro, waste-to-energy and storage such as batteries, flywheels and vehicle-to-grid; they typically have high capital cost per kilowatt.
Integrating distributed sources raises technical problems of power quality, voltage stability, harmonics, reliability, protection and control; IEEE 1547 sets the interconnection standard.
Local production avoids transmission losses, which are generally 8-15% of energy on long lines and transformers.
Solar-plus-battery stand-alone systems have a low levelized cost, so some authors think they may enable mass grid defection.
A single vendor's vulnerable control system used at thousands of sites could let one attacker disable them all, reversing decentralisation's benefits.

definition.text: A localized grouping of generation, storage and loads that normally runs connected to the main grid but can disconnect and operate autonomously.

facts.text: A microgrid links to the macrogrid at a single point of common coupling, which can be disconnected.
Generation and loads in a microgrid are usually interconnected at low voltage and can run on DC, AC or both.

definition.text: The process of producing electric power from primary energy sources, carried out in power stations before delivery or storage.

facts.text: Electricity is not freely available in nature and must be produced by transforming other forms of energy; most is made by electromechanical generators driven by heat engines, flowing water or wind.
Only photovoltaic solar and fuel cells produce commercial-scale electricity without a generator; almost all other commercial power comes from a turbine.
World generation in 2024 was 30,850 TWh: coal 34%, gas 22%, hydro 14%, nuclear 9%, wind 8%, solar 7%, oil and other fossil 3%, biomass 2%.
Cleanliness depends on the source: fossil fuels supply about 10% of electricity in France, 70% in the US and 80% in China.
Coal plants supply about a third of world electricity but cause the most early deaths per unit of energy, mainly from air pollution.
Gas plants are more efficient than coal and emit less carbon dioxide, but gas extraction releases significant methane.
Hydropower supplied 15% of world electricity in 2023 and, with a dam and reservoir, can change output within seconds or minutes.
Grids carry varying loads; the daily minimum is the base load, often supplied by plants that run continuously.

definition.text: An upgrade of the 20th-century electrical grid that uses two-way communications and distributed intelligent devices.

facts.text: Classic grids were centralized, one-way systems of transmission, distribution and demand-driven control; two-way flows of electricity and information could improve delivery.
Smart grids use techniques such as state estimation to detect faults and self-heal without technician intervention, improving reliability and reducing vulnerability to disasters or attacks.
They handle bidirectional flows from rooftop solar and electric-car batteries; classic grids assumed one-way flow, so local over-generation can raise safety issues.
Smart grid flexibility allows more variable renewables such as solar and wind, even without added storage.
Demand response lets generators and loads coordinate in real time to flatten spikes, avoiding reserve generators and letting users run low-priority devices when energy is cheapest.
Smart grids let suppliers and consumers exchange price and willingness-to-pay signals, so only critical loads pay peak prices.
Concerns centre on smart meters and their remote control and variable pricing, on cyberattack vulnerability, and on the need for a business case before a utility invests.
